title: How extreme rain is putting orangutans at risk
description:
Orangutans are the world’s most endangered apes and they’re now even closer to extinction. They live on two islands in southeast Asia: Sumatra and Borneo. In November, an extreme weather event in the area killed more than 1,000 people there, plus about 7% of the world’s rarest type of orangutan according to a new study.

BBC Climate and Science reporter Georgina Rannard takes us through how orangutans are being pushed towards extinction and what some countries and charities are doing to protect them.

We also hear from a conservationist making an effort to save the species.

summaryZh: 本集探討紅毛猩猩在蘇門答臘與婆羅洲的瀕危現況。三個物種為婆羅洲、蘇門答臘與塔帕努里，後者約 800 隻，是最為瀕危的。族群數量自一百年前約 230,000 隻驟減，目前婆羅洲約 104,000 隻、蘇門答臘約 14,000 隻；每年約有 2,000–3,000 隻被殺，生育間隔約 7–8 年，使得即使每年損失 1% 也會加速滅絕。主要威脅包括為種植棕櫚油、採礦、伐木與興建水電而大規模砍伐和破碎化棲地，另有偷捕寵物貿易與人獸衝突。報導指出去年 11 月的極端豪雨造成超過 1,000 人死亡，並造成約 58 隻塔帕努里死亡，約佔其族群的 7% 。保育工作包括設立保護區、復育與基因保護計畫，以及鼓勵由富國付費以保留森林的國際方案。
summaryEn: The episode explains how orangutans — living on Sumatra and Borneo in three species (Bornean, Sumatran and the critically endangered Tapanuli) — are being driven closer to extinction. Populations have fallen from roughly 230,000 a century ago to about 104,000 Bornean, 14,000 Sumatran and roughly 800 Tapanuli; some 2,000–3,000 orangutans are killed each year and females reproduce only every 7–8 years. Key threats are habitat loss from palm‑oil plantations, mining, logging, hydropower and peatland drainage, plus illegal pet trade and human–wildlife conflict. A November extreme rainfall event killed over 1,000 people and about 58 Tapanuli (≈7% of that species), showing how extreme weather can push small populations toward extinction. Conservation efforts include protected areas, rehabilitation and genetic programs, and international payment schemes to keep forests standing.
